source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Part I: Trend Reversals: A Trend Becoming an Opposite Trend

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same. Helpers: body(i)=|close[i]-open[i]|; range(i)=high[i]-low[i]; avgBody(n)/avgRange(n) = plain means over bars 1..n; ema(n); tick = instrument minimum move; swingHigh/swingLow(strength) = a confirmed pivot needing `strength` weaker bars on both sides; highest(x,n,k)/lowest(x,n,k) = extreme of x over n bars ending k bars ago (k=1 excludes the current bar); countLegs/pushCount = alternating-pivot counters. This is Part I's long, largely discursive introduction: a mix of durable mechanical principles (trend-line breaks, leg counting, measured moves, stop placement) and long stretches of institutional/fundamental theory and multi-figure chart narratives (Figures PI.1-PI.5, not reproduced in the text) that restate the same handful of primitives via unlabeled bar numbers. Candidates mechanize the general principle each passage states; repeated restatements of the same idea are cited once with every page it recurs on rather than duplicated.

candidates.name: TrendLineBreakRequiredForReversal
candidates.quote: The single most important rule in these books is that you should never be thinking about trading against a trend until after there has been a breakout of the channel, which means a break beyond a significant trend line.
candidates.description: Context filter: a countertrend/reversal entry is only considered after price has broken beyond the trend line of the established trend (a channel breakout).
candidates.pseudocode: trendLineBreak(direction, breakBars, breakTicks*tick) // close beyond the projected trend line (from swing pivots) for breakBars consecutive bars by breakTicks

complexity.reason: needs trend-line projection from swing-pivot detection, then a toleranced break test

notes: The single most repeated principle in the chapter; cited pages are representative, not exhaustive.

candidates.name: StrongReversalBarShape
candidates.quote: Also, you should take a reversal trade only if there is a strong signal bar. You need evidence that the other side is strong enough to have a chance of taking control.
candidates.description: Primitive: the reversal's signal bar must be a strong trend bar in the new direction - large body relative to its range, small tails.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && body(0) >= bodyFraction * range(0) && (high[0]-close[0]) <= tailFraction*range(0) && (open[0]-low[0]) <= tailFraction*range(0)
candidates.book_order_type: buy/sell stop one tick beyond the signal bar

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on open/high/low/close

candidates.name: TestOfOldTrendExtremeAfterBreak
candidates.quote: The second requirement happens most of the time, but is not required: after the trend line break, the market comes back and successfully tests the extreme of the old trend.
candidates.description: After a trend-line break, require price to move back and trade at/near the old trend's swing extreme before treating the follow-through as a qualifying reversal setup.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(extreme(0) - oldTrendExtreme) <= toleranceTicks * tick // oldTrendExtreme = the swing extreme that stood before the trend-line break

complexity.reason: needs the pre-break swing extreme tracked and a toleranced level test against it

candidates.name: DoubleFailedTestTriesOpposite
candidates.quote: whenever the market tries to do something twice and fails, it usually tries the opposite.
candidates.description: After two separate failed attempts to break through the same price level within the lookback, treat a subsequent move away from that level as a higher-probability entry in the opposite direction.
candidates.pseudocode: countFailedAttempts(level, lookback, toleranceTicks) >= 2 && close[0] moves away from level in the opposite direction
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry beyond the bar that confirms the move away from the level

complexity.reason: needs a tracked price level plus a counter of distinct failed attempts against it

candidates.name: MinimumLegLengthForReversal
candidates.quote: Most traders prefer to see at least five bars or so [in both the trend-line-break leg and the test leg].
candidates.description: Both the leg that breaks the trend line and the leg that tests the old extreme should each be at least minLegBars bars long for the reversal to be considered credible.
candidates.pseudocode: barsSinceLastSwingPivot(breakLegStart) >= minLegBars && barsSinceLastSwingPivot(testLegStart) >= minLegBars

complexity.reason: bar counts since the last swing pivot, once pivots are available

notes: Brooks explicitly allows exceptions when one leg has one or two exceptionally large bars.

candidates.name: TrailStopToRecentSwingPullback
candidates.quote: After the market moves above the high of the first leg up, bulls will move their protective stops up to just below this higher low.
candidates.description: Trail the protective stop to just below (long) / above (short) the most recent confirmed swing pullback once a new trend-leg extreme is exceeded; the same logic also sets the initial stop beyond the swing point that began the current spike.
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = lowest(low, sinceLastSwingLow) - stopOffsetTicks * tick // mirrored for shorts using the most recent swing high
candidates.book_order_type: resting stop order, trailed as new swing pullbacks confirm

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection plus persistent per-position stop state

notes: Covers both the initial 'ideal stop beyond the most recent spike' (p70) and the trailing form (p73-74); same underlying primitive at two different times.

candidates.name: MeasuredMoveOfCounterTrendBar
candidates.quote: The first target is the high of the bear trend bar, and the next target is a measured move up, equal to the height of the bear trend bar.
candidates.description: When fading a countertrend bar, target 1 is that bar's far extreme; target 2 projects the bar's own height an additional multiple beyond target 1.
candidates.pseudocode: target1 = high[signalBarOffset]; target2 = high[signalBarOffset] + (high[signalBarOffset] - low[signalBarOffset]) * multiple

complexity.reason: arithmetic on one prior bar's range projected from its extreme

candidates.name: StopSizedToCounterTrendBarRange
candidates.quote: Some traders will use an initial protective stop that is about the same number of ticks as the bear trend bar is tall, and others will use their usual stop, like two points in the Emini.
candidates.description: Place the protective stop at a distance about equal to the faded countertrend bar's own high-low range, rather than a fixed tick amount.
candidates.pseudocode: stopDistance = stopFraction * range(signalBarOffset)

complexity.reason: single-bar range arithmetic

candidates.name: FadeLargeCounterTrendBarInTrend
candidates.quote: if there is a bull trend and it forms a large bear trend bar closing on its low, most traders will expect this reversal attempt to fail, and many will buy at the close of the bear bar.
candidates.description: In an established trend, when a large countertrend trend bar forms and closes on its extreme, enter with the trend at the close of that bar / just beyond its extreme, betting the countertrend attempt fails.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] < open[0] && body(0) >= bodyMultiple * avgBody(lookback) && close[0] <= low[0] + closeTolerance * range(0) // entered at close (market) or on a stop below low[0]; established uptrend context assumed via a separate trend filter
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the close of the bar and/or on a stop one tick below its low

complexity.reason: window average of bodies plus a close-position test on the signal bar

candidates.likely_existing_rule: ReversalBarBodyAboveAverage (V02-02), applied to the opposite (fade) trend context

candidates.name: OutsideBarPattern
candidates.quote: One of the failed short entries often quickly becomes a strong outside up bar.
candidates.description: Primitive: the current bar's range fully engulfs the prior bar's range (an outside bar) and closes up, a classic bull-reversal bar variant.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] > high[1] && low[0] < low[1] && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the outside bar's high

complexity.reason: two-bar range comparison

candidates.name: SecondEntryFailureBreakout
candidates.quote: Once it does fail, traders will see this failed low 2 as a failed bear flag, and it often leads to a strong breakout to the upside.
candidates.description: After a Low2 (or High2) pullback entry fails to trigger/follow through within a few bars, treat the subsequent breakout in the trend's new direction as a high-confidence signal.
candidates.pseudocode: pullbackEntryOrdinal(direction, sinceTrendStart) == 2 && no trigger/follow-through within windowBars && breakout(oppositeDirection) triggers
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry beyond the breakout bar

complexity.reason: depends on the same stateful pullback-ordinal counter as V01-05, plus a failure/timeout test

candidates.name: AlwaysInDirectionFlip
candidates.quote: A reversal at some point makes the majority of traders believe that the always-in position has reversed, and this almost always requires some kind of breakout.
candidates.description: Concept: a formal notion of the market's assumed always-in direction, which flips on sufficiently strong breakouts/spikes; used throughout the book to gate reversal conviction but never reduced to a bar-level test.
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - design-level concept referenced by many other candidates as alwaysInDirection()

complexity.reason: explicitly called out in MINING.md as a concept needing a design decision before it is codable

notes: The single most recurring concept in this chapter; defined once here for the whole file.

candidates.name: UndercutAndReverseWithinBars
candidates.quote: sometimes the pullback extends below the low of the bear trend, running stops on the new longs. If this lower low reverses back up within a few bars, it can lead to a strong swing up.
candidates.description: Price briefly undercuts a recent swing low by a small amount then closes back above it within reverseBars bars - a stop-run/undercut reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: exists k in 0..reverseBars-1: low[k] < priorSwingLow - undercutTicks*tick && close[0] > priorSwingLow
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the reversal bar that closes back above the prior swing low

complexity.reason: a tracked swing low plus a small window comparison

candidates.name: ExcessiveUndercutMeansNewLegDown
candidates.quote: If, in contrast, the lower low extends too far below the prior low, it is better to assume that the bear trend has begun a new leg down
candidates.description: Suppress the undercut-and-reverse entry (VP1-13) when the undercut exceeds a larger threshold, since that is read as a genuine new leg rather than a stop run.
candidates.pseudocode: (priorSwingLow - low[0]) > excessiveMultiple * undercutTicks * tick // when true, do not fire VP1-13

complexity.reason: same tracked level as VP1-13 with a larger threshold

candidates.name: TrendChannelLineOvershootReversal
candidates.quote: One trend will often end with a trend channel line overshoot and reversal followed by a two-legged move that breaks the trend line.
candidates.description: Price briefly exceeds (overshoots) the trend channel line (the parallel line on the far side of the channel from the trend line) then reverses back inside the channel - an early warning of trend exhaustion.
candidates.pseudocode: high[1] > channelLine(1) && close[0] < channelLine(0) // channelLine projected parallel to the trend line through the opposite extremes; mirrored for bear channels
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context/pattern signal, feeds an Entry elsewhere)

complexity.reason: needs both trend-line and parallel channel-line projection from swing pivots

candidates.name: ThreePushWedgePattern
candidates.quote: Bar 29 was the third push in a small wedge
candidates.description: Primitive: the market has formed three sequential swing extremes in the same direction, each extending beyond the last, typically with converging trend lines (a wedge).
candidates.pseudocode: pushCount(direction, pivotStrength) >= 3

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and extreme comparison across three legs

notes: Same underlying primitive as ThreePushesWedgePattern in 01_example_of_how_to_trade_a_reversal.json; defined independently per chapter per convention.

candidates.name: ExpandingTriangleTopBottom
candidates.quote: It was also a small expanding triangle top (bars 6, 7, 8, 11, and 12).
candidates.description: Primitive: a series of alternating swing highs and lows that progressively diverge (each new push further than the last on both sides) - the opposite of a wedge's convergence.
candidates.pseudocode: swingHigh(k) > swingHigh(k-2) && swingLow(k) < swingLow(k-2) for the last pushCount alternating pivots

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and comparison of alternating highs and lows across several pushes

candidates.name: ShavedBarPattern
candidates.quote: It had great momentum and a shaved top and bottom, meaning that the bulls were extremely aggressive and higher prices should follow.
candidates.description: Primitive: a trend bar with (near) zero tails at both ends - the open sits at the bar's low and the close at its high (bull case), a stronger variant of a strong trend bar.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && (open[0] - low[0]) <= tailToleranceTicks*tick && (high[0] - close[0]) <= tailToleranceTicks*tick
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification, strengthens a signal-bar or momentum test)

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on open/high/low/close

candidates.name: ShrinkingBodiesInSpike
candidates.quote: The bull bodies became progressively smaller in the spike, and this was a sign of a loss of momentum.
candidates.description: Filter: the last three same-direction trend bars have monotonically shrinking bodies, signaling loss of momentum within a spike (a wedge-shaped body sequence, ahead of a possible reversal or pause).
candidates.pseudocode: close[2]>open[2] && close[1]>open[1] && close[0]>open[0] && body(2) > body(1) && body(1) > body(0)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter/warning, feeds an Exit or a reversal Entry elsewhere)

complexity.reason: three-bar comparison of body sizes

candidates.name: ConsecutiveClimaxCorrection
candidates.quote: Consecutive buy climaxes usually are followed by a protracted correction that has at least two legs.
candidates.description: After climaxNumber consecutive climax spikes (each a strong breakout with minimal intervening pullback) in the same direction, expect/require at least a minCorrectionBars-bar, two-legged correction - used to suppress fresh with-trend entries or favor countertrend scalps until the correction plays out. A climax signals an expected pause, not necessarily a trend reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: climaxCount(sinceSessionStart, maxPullbackTicks) >= climaxNumber // suppresses with-trend Entry candidates until countLegs(sinceLastClimax) >= 2 and barsSince(lastClimax) >= minCorrectionBars

complexity.reason: climax identification and leg counting are both design decisions Brooks does not reduce to a fixed test

candidates.name: MeasuringGapProjection
candidates.quote: This gap could function as a measuring gap, and the low of the start of the leg up from bar 4 to the middle of the measuring gap projected up to just below the bar 7 high.
candidates.description: Target: mirror the distance from the start of the current leg to a measuring gap's midpoint, projected an equal distance beyond the midpoint.
candidates.pseudocode: target = gapMidpoint + (gapMidpoint - legStartPrice) // mirrored sign for a bear leg

complexity.reason: needs gap detection and leg-start tracking

candidates.name: Leg1EqualsLeg2MeasuredMove
candidates.quote: A strong spike usually leads to a measured move, and here there was a leg 1 = leg 2 move down to bar 15 where leg 2 ... was just a little larger than leg 1 down to bar 13.
candidates.description: Target: project the first leg's length again from the pullback extreme that ended it, so the second leg is expected to about equal the first.
candidates.pseudocode: target = leg1PullbackExtreme - (leg1Start - leg1End) // mirrored sign for an up-leg

complexity.reason: needs leg1's start/end endpoints from swing-pivot detection

candidates.name: CloseAboveSwingHighSignOfStrength
candidates.quote: Anytime the market goes above a swing high, it is a sign of strength, even if that high was in the prior down move and not part of a series of higher highs in an uptrend.
candidates.description: Closing above any recent swing high (even one from the opposite prior trend) is a bullish strength signal, usable as a context filter favoring long entries.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > swingHigh(pivotStrength, lookback)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection, though the fixed-window variant is simpler

notes: A fixed-window Highest(High,N)[1] version already exists in the catalog; the swing-pivot version is Brooks's stricter reading.

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutBecomesPullbackInNewTrend
candidates.quote: Remember, any failed breakout that fails in its attempt to resume the trend becomes a breakout pullback in the new trend.
candidates.description: When a breakout in the direction of the OLD trend fails (reverses back through its own starting point) after a trend-line break, treat the failure/reversal bar as a breakout-pullback entry in the NEW (opposite) direction.
candidates.pseudocode: trendLineBreak(direction) already true && breakoutAttempt(oldDirection) closes back beyond its own start // Entry(newDirection) at the next open
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry beyond the reversal bar that fails the old-direction breakout

complexity.reason: needs the old breakout's starting point tracked and a failure test against it

candidates.name: ConsecutiveAdverseCloseExit
candidates.quote: Bulls will sometimes allow one bar to go against them, but most would not allow two when the original buy signal was weak and the bar 33 bull breakout did not have any follow-through.
candidates.description: Exit the position if adverseBars consecutive bars close against it - a tighter tolerance than a full stop, meant for positions taken on a weak original signal.
candidates.pseudocode: countif(i in 0..adverseBars-1, close[i] < open[i]) == adverseBars // long; mirrored for shorts
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (discretionary exit at the market or on a stop)

complexity.reason: fixed window CountIF over bar closes

candidates.likely_existing_rule: ConsecutiveCloseExit is the same shape in the favorable direction; this is the adverse-direction analog

candidates.name: BothSidesValidMeansTradingRange
candidates.quote: Both the bull and bear cases were valid, which usually means that the market is in a trading range, which it was.
candidates.description: Concept: when comparably strong bull and bear arguments coexist, the market is probably in a trading range rather than trending - useful as a context switch between trend-following and range-scalping rule sets, but not yet a bar-level test.
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - classification concept, needs a trading-range definition

complexity.reason: "the market is in a trading range" is one of MINING.md's own examples of a concept needing a design decision

candidates.name: TradingRangeBreakoutWithTrendBias
candidates.quote: you should expect the breakout from the trading range to be in the direction of the trend because that is what happens in about 80 percent of cases... All head and shoulders tops and bottoms are really head and shoulders continuation patterns (flags).
candidates.description: Treat an apparent reversal-shaped trading range (double top/bottom, head and shoulders, triangle, wedge) as more likely (Brooks estimates ~80%) to break out WITH the larger trend than against it; needs pattern-shape recognition and a trading-range definition, a design decision.
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - classification/bias concept over a detected trading range and its shape

complexity.reason: requires a trading-range detector plus shape classification before any bar-level test is possible

candidates.name: IntradaySessionCloseStrengthBias
candidates.quote: When the market is in a bull trend on the higher time frame charts, the 5 minute chart often has a rally into the close, and the bar of the daily chart has a higher chance of being a bull trend bar.
candidates.description: Strength or weakness in the final closingWindowMinutes of today's session biases the odds for tomorrow's/the next higher-timeframe bar's trend direction; usable as a next-session context filter.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] near highest(high, closingWindowBars, 0) at session end // sets a persistent bullish-bias flag consulted at the next session's entries
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter carried across a session boundary)

complexity.reason: needs session-end detection and state carried across the session boundary

candidates.name: BreakevenStopAfterMomentumConfirmation
candidates.quote: After the strong bull spike formed at bar 21, the bulls would have moved their stop to one tick below its low, which was just about breakeven.
candidates.description: Once a strong momentum trend bar confirms the new trend while a position is open, move the protective stop to breakeven (or just beyond that confirming bar's near extreme).
candidates.pseudocode: if StrongTrendBar(0) in position direction && ctx.MarketPosition() != 0: newStop = max(currentStop, low[0] - offsetTicks*tick) // mirrored for shorts

complexity.reason: single-bar strength test plus position-state-gated stop adjustment

candidates.name: MicroChannelWeakensReversalOdds
candidates.quote: the micro channel down from bar 29 was so tight that the probability of success was not high [for the reversal attempt].
candidates.description: Concept: a reversal attempt against a tight micro-channel (a run of small, overlapping, persistently same-direction bars) has lower odds; needs a micro-channel detector before it is codable.
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - classification concept (micro-channel = a run of small-range, minimally-overlapping same-direction bars)

complexity.reason: micro-channel detection is a pattern-recognition design decision, not a fixed test

candidates.name: PriceGapNoOverlap
candidates.quote: After the next bar closed and its low was above the bar 5 high, bar 6 became a gap and a possible measuring gap.
candidates.description: Primitive: the current bar's low trades entirely above the referenced bar's high (a true price gap, no overlap), confirming breakout strength and flagging a possible measuring gap.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] > high[gapBarOffset] // bull gap; mirrored: high[0] < low[gapBarOffset] for a bear gap

complexity.reason: two-bar range comparison

candidates.name: FinalFlagReversalSetup
candidates.quote: Many upside breakouts of bull flags soon reverse down and then the market breaks to the downside, creating a reversal. When that happens, the bull flag becomes the final flag in the bull trend.
candidates.description: Concept: a final flag is the last, often small/tight consolidation before an extended trend exhausts and reverses; it is identifiable mainly in hindsight (once the subsequent breakout fails), so a prospective rule needs a design decision (e.g., a small 1-3 bar flag after an extended trend with a tight micro-channel).
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - classification concept, circular without a forward-looking proxy

complexity.reason: the defining feature (this flag turns out to be the last one) is only knowable after the fact

candidates.name: DuelingLinesPattern
candidates.quote: The market will probably form a dueling lines bottom around the bull trend line drawn below the bars 1, 2, and 4 lows... and the trend channel line drawn below the bars 9 and 13 lows.
candidates.description: Concept: a reversal setting up where two independently drawn trend/channel lines from different pivots converge near the same price - a named Brooks pattern combining two trend-line projections, which needs a design decision to formalize.
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - classification concept over two independently projected lines

complexity.reason: combines two trend-line projections plus a convergence/coincidence test that Brooks does not quantify

rejected.quote: Institutional trading is done by discretionary traders and computers... Since the majority of the volume is now traded by HFT firms... a single institution cannot move the market very far or for very long.
rejected.reason: institutional/fundamental market-structure theory; not decidable from OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: Just look at correlated markets, like the Emini and all of the related exchange-traded funds (ETFs) like the SPY, and you will see that they basically move tick for tick.
rejected.reason: requires another instrument's price series, explicitly out of scope

rejected.quote: Significant tops in the S&P are often presaged by a big down day or two in a bellwether stock like Apple (AAPL).
rejected.reason: requires another symbol's data, explicitly out of scope

rejected.quote: They do not accept that it is all math and has nothing to do with fairness or emotion... That is the day when they stop losing money.
rejected.reason: trader psychology/emotion narrative, not a bar-level test

rejected.quote: If traders win four points in four out of 10 trades, they have 16 points of profit off of their swing trades... an average of 1.6 points of profit per trade.
rejected.reason: illustrative trade-expectancy arithmetic, not itself a decidable entry/exit condition

rejected.quote: the first big pullback in a strong trend usually tests the 15 minute moving average.
rejected.reason: requires a second, higher-timeframe bar series not necessarily available to a single-timeframe strategy

rejected.quote: Newsletter writers who make their living by selling fear will make a fortune by scaring people into believing that the Dow will fall for a measured move down to below 1,000.
rejected.reason: commentary on news/newsletter behavior, not decidable from bars

chapter_summary: Part I's introduction: a long mix of durable mechanical principles (never trade countertrend before a trend-line break, insist on a strong signal bar and a test of the old extreme, leg-length minimums, stop placement beyond the recent swing point, measured-move and leg1=leg2 targets, wedge/expanding-triangle/double-top pivot counting) and extended institutional-fundamentals theory plus five large unreproduced-figure chart narratives (PI.1-PI.5) that mostly restate the same primitives via specific unlabeled bars. Genuinely new, concrete additions beyond chapter 02 and the example chapter are the outside-bar and shaved-bar patterns, shrinking-bodies-in-a-spike, the adverse-close-count exit, the gap-no-overlap primitive, and the breakeven-after-momentum-confirmation stop move. Always-in direction, trading-range classification, final-flag identification, dueling lines, and micro-channel detection all recur constantly through the book and are honestly flagged research since Brooks never reduces them to a bar-level test - later chapters likely refine some of these. Institutional/HFT/fundamental theory, cross-symbol comparisons (AAPL vs. SPY, ETF correlation), trader psychology, and multi-timeframe EMA tests were rejected as outside the engine's inputs.
